articles.title: Google made a watermark for AI images that you can’t edit out
articles.summary: Google is rolling SynthID out to Cloud customers using Vertex AI and the Imagen image creation tool so it can see how the unobtrusive watermark works in the wild.
articles.body: The Google DeepMind team has believed for years that building great generative AI tools also requires building great tools to detect what has been created by AI. There are plenty of obvious, high-stakes reasons why, says Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis. “Every time we talk about it and other systems, it’s, ‘What about the problem of deepfakes?’” With another contentious election season coming in 2024 in both the US and the UK, Hassabis says that building systems to identify and detect AI imagery is more important all the time. Hassabis and his team have been working on a tool for the last few years, which Google is releasing publicly today. It’s called SynthID, and it’s designed to essentially watermark an AI-generated image in a way that is imperceptible to the human eye but easily caught by a dedicated AI detection tool. The watermark is embedded in the pixels of the image, but Hassabis says it doesn’t alter the image itself in any noticeable way. “It doesn’t change the image, the quality of the image, or the experience of it,” he says. “But it’s robust to various transformations — cropping, resizing, all of the things that you might do to try and get around normal, traditional, simple watermarks.” As SynthID’s underlying models improve, Hassabis says, the watermark will be even less perceptible to humans but even more easily detected by DeepMind’s tools. That’s as technical as Hassabis and Google DeepMind want to be for now. Even the launch blog post is sparse on details because SynthID is still a new system. “The more you reveal about the way it works, the easier it’ll be for hackers and nefarious entities to get around it,” Hassabis says. SynthID is rolling out first in a Google-centric way: Google Cloud customers who use the company’s Vertex AI platform and the Imagen image generator will be able to embed and detect the watermark. As the system gets more real-world testing, Hassabis hopes it’ll get better. Then Google will be able to use it in more places, share more about how it works, and get even more data on how it works. [Image: Google’s SynthID tools will tell you how likely it is an image was AI-generated. Eventually, Hassabis seems to hope SynthID might be something like an internet-wide standard. The foundational ideas could even be used in other media like video and text. Once Google has proven the tech, “the question is scaling it up, sharing it with other partners that want it, and then scaling up the consumer solution — and then having that debate with civil society about where we want to take this.” He says over and over that this is a beta test, a first try at a new thing, “and not a silver bullet to the deepfake problem.” But he clearly thinks it could be huge. Of course, Google’s not the only company with this particular ambition. Far from it. Just last month, Meta, OpenAI, Google, and several of the other biggest names in AI promised to build in more protections and safety systems for their AI. A number of companies are also working with a protocol called C2PA, which uses cryptographic metadata to tag AI-generated content. Google is, in many ways, playing catch-up on all its AI tools, including detection. And it seems likely that we’re going to get too many AI-detection standards before we get the ones that actually work. But Hassabis is confident that watermarking is at least going to be part of the answer around the web. SynthID is launching during Google’s Cloud Next conference, in which the company tells its business customers about new features in Google’s Cloud and Workspace products. Thomas Kurian, Google Cloud’s CEO, says that usage of the Vertex AI platform is absolutely exploding: “The models are getting more and more sophisticated, and we’ve had a huge, huge ramp in the number of people using the models.” That growth and the improvement in the SynthID system made Kurian and Hassabis feel this was the time to launch. Customers are definitely worried about deepfakes, Kurian says, but they also have much more mundane AI detection needs. “We have a lot of customers who use these tools to create images for ad copy,” he says by way of example, “and they want to verify the original image because many times the marketing department has a central team that actually creates the original blueprint image.” Retail is another big one: some retailers are using AI tools to generate descriptions for their huge catalog of products, and they need to make sure the product photos they’re uploading don’t get mixed up with the generated images they’re using for brainstorming and iteration purposes. (You might already be seeing DeepMind-created descriptions like this, by the way, both on retail websites and in places like YouTube Shorts.) They may not be quite as viscerally important as fake Trump mug shots or a swagged-out pope, but these are the ways AI is already showing up in day-to-day business. One thing Kurian says he’s looking for as SynthID rolls out — other than whether the system, you know, works — is how and where people want to use it. He’s pretty sure Slides and Docs will need SynthID integration, for one. “When you’re using Slides, you want to know where you’re deriving images from.” But where else? Hassabis suggests SynthID could eventually be offered as a Chrome extension or even built into the browser so it can identify generated images all over the web. But let’s say that happens: should the tool proactively flag everything that might be generated or wait for some kind of query from the user? Is a huge red triangle the right way to say “this was made with AI,” or should it be something more subtle? Kurian suggests that there might ultimately be lots of user experience options. As long as the underlying tech works consistently, he figures, users could choose how exactly they want it to appear. It could even vary by topic: maybe you don’t much care if the Slides background you’re using was created by humans or AI, but “if you’re in hospitals scanning tumors, you really want to make sure that was not a synthetically generated image.” The launch of any AI detection tool is guaranteed to be the start of an arms race. In many cases, a losing one: OpenAI has already given up on a tool meant to detect text written by its own ChatGPT chatbot. If SynthID catches on, it will only inspire hackers and developers to find creative ways around the system, which will force Google DeepMind to improve the system, and round and round they’ll go. Hassabis says, with only a smidge of resignation, that the team is ready for that. “It will probably have to be a live solution that we have to update,” he says, “more like antivirus or something like that. You’re always going to have to be alert to a new type of attack and new type of transform.” For now, that’s still a far-off problem because the whole initial system of AI image creation, use, and detection is controlled by Google. But DeepMind built this with the whole internet in mind, and Hassabis says he’s ready for the long journey of bringing SynthID everywhere it needs to be. But then he catches himself — one thing at a time, he says. “It would be premature to think about the scaling and the civil society debates until we’ve proven out that the foundational piece of the technology works.” That’s the first job and the reason SynthID is launching now. If and when SynthID or something like it really works, then we can start to figure out what it means for life online.

articles.title: The web has a new system for making AI companies pay up
articles.summary: A new licensing standard, called the RSL Standard, aims to allow AI companies to license content from across the web. Reddit, Yahoo, Quora, and others are already on board.
articles.body: A new licensing standard aims to let web publishers set the terms of how AI system developers use their work. On Wednesday, major brands like Reddit, Yahoo, Medium, Quora, and People Inc. announced support for Really Simple Licensing (RSL), an open content licensing standard that enables publishers to outline how bots should pay to scrape their sites for AI training data. They’re hoping the collective action gives them leverage to get AI companies on board. The RSL Standard builds upon the robots.txt protocol, which has long allowed publishers to provide instructions to web crawlers about what parts of their site they can and can’t access. But instead of just saying yes or no to specific bots, websites can now add licensing and royalty terms to their robots.txt file. They can also embed the terms in online books, videos, and training datasets that they may want compensation for. Behind the RSL Standard is a newly formed rights organization called the RSL Collective, helmed by Eckart Walther, a co-creator of the Really Simple Syndication (RSS) standard and former CardSpring CEO, and Doug Leeds, the former CEO of IAC Publishing and Ask.com. “The goal is to create a new, scalable business model for the web,” Walther tells The Verge. “RSL takes some of those early RSS ideas and creates a new layer for the entire internet where licensing rights and compensation rights are defined.” The RSL Standard supports a variety of licensing models, including free ones. Site owners can ask AI companies to pay a subscription or assign a pay-per-crawl fee through the RSL Standard, which companies must pay each time an AI bot crawls the website. They can also implement a pay-per-inference fee, allowing sites to receive compensation when an AI model references their work to generate a response. Bots that are crawling sites for other purposes, like archival or search engine inclusion, can proceed as usual. Several media companies, including The Verge parent company Vox Media, The Wall Street Journal owner News Corp, and The New York Times, have struck licensing agreements with individual AI companies such as OpenAI and Amazon. But the RSL Collective aims to simplify this process by allowing any website owner or creator to get paid for their work rather than negotiating separate deals. Like a lot of standards, RSL’s success depends on major industry players — in this case, AI companies — buying into it. AI model builders have repeatedly been accused of ignoring sites’ robots.txt files, and there’s no simple way to tally something like the inference fee without their participation. The RSL Collective is betting that bringing together some of the biggest web publishers will make adopting the standard more appealing. “Our job is to go out and get a big group of people to say it’s in your interest, both efficiently, because you can negotiate with everybody at once, and legally, because if you don’t, you’re violating everybody at once,” Leeds says. The RSL Standard by itself also can’t block bots from visiting a website, unlike the “pay per crawl” system already offered by Cloudflare. The RSL Collective is currently working with Fastly, a content delivery network, to admit AI bots to websites based on whether they’ve agreed to license content. Fastly is “the bouncer at the door to the club, and they won’t let people in unless they have the right ID,” Leeds says. “RSL is issuing the IDs. So we say, ‘Hey, you’ve agreed to license this content,’ and Fastly says, ‘Come on, in your ID checks out.’” Publishers who don’t use Fastly can still ask AI companies to license their content, but they’ll be unable to block AI crawlers until more providers build a solution. Leeds believes that the RSL Collective can legally enforce licenses as well, as he says “all participants in the collective rights organization participate in the enforcement of any infringement,” spreading the legal costs. He compares the system to existing digital rights organizations, like the music rights group ASCAP, which collects licensing fees and distributes them to members. While conventional music licensing benefits from a particularly strong and well-established legal precedent for copyright protection, however, unauthorized scraping and the use of media for training AI systems still land in a legal gray area, with major AI players currently fighting lawsuits from Reddit, Getty Images, and many online publishers. “There has always been a question of whether bots have agreed to terms that they don’t see,” Leeds and Walther added in an emailed statement. “RSL changes that fundamentally, putting crawlers on notice of what the terms are before they access a site.” Even so, Leeds hopes the system can create an intuitive way to navigate licensing works for AI training. “What we’re doing is not reinventing wheels or inventing wheels — we’re just bringing them to a place that they haven’t existed before,” Leeds says. “The reason they haven’t existed here before is because they haven’t had a standard that we could build on. So that’s why RSL Standard is so important: it gives the infrastructure to then create the things that have worked in every other media industry that hasn’t happened yet.” The RSL Collective is free for publishers and creators to join, with other big brands like O’Reilly, wikiHow, and IGN owner Ziff Davis also on board.

articles.title: A pay-to-scrape AI licensing standard is now official
articles.summary: A licensing standard aimed at making AI companies pay for the content they scrape across the web is now official. With the publication of the RSL 1.0 spec, publishers can dictate licensing rules and indicate whether they want their content to appear in AI search.
articles.body: An open licensing standard that aims to make AI companies pay for the content they vacuum up across the web is now an official specification. Really Simple Licensing 1.0 — or RSL for short — gives publishers the ability to dictate licensing and compensation rules to the web crawlers that visit their sites. The RSL Collective announced the standard in September with backing from Yahoo, Ziff Davis, and O’Reilly Media. It’s an expansion of the robots.txt file, which outlines the parts of a website a web crawler can access. Though RSL alone can’t block AI scrapers that don’t pay for a license, the web infrastructure providers that support the standard can — a list that now includes Cloudflare and Akamai, in addition to Fastly. RSL’s 1.0 release lets publishers block their content from AI-powered search features, like Google’s AI Mode, while maintaining a presence in traditional search results. Currently, Google doesn’t give websites an individual option to opt out of AI-powered features without booting them out of traditional search, too. “RSL provides exactly that missing layer,” RSL Collective cofounders Doug Leeds and Eckart Walther say in an emailed statement to The Verge. “Using RSL, Google can respect a publisher’s preferences at the use case level, which means a publisher can stay fully available in traditional search, while opting out of AI training, grounding, or generative answers.” Google is currently facing an investigation from the European Commission, which is looking into whether the company has violated antitrust policies by using web publishers’ content in AI search features “without offering them the possibility to refuse such use of their content.” The RSL Collective says more than 1,500 media organizations and brands now support RSL. In addition to Reddit, Quora, WikiHow, Stack Overflow, and Medium, publishers like The Associated Press, Vox Media (The Verge’s parent company), The Guardian, Slate, BuzzFeed, and Men’s Journal publisher Arena Group have also endorsed the standard. “With this release, and the support for it across the internet ecosystem, RSL 1.0 becomes the expected and trusted way to communicate how content may be used in AI systems, giving those signals real weight in both practice and legal interpretation,” Leeds says. The RSL Collective also worked with the Creative Commons to add a new “contribution” payment option for nonprofit organizations and individuals behind the webpages, code repositories, and datasets that make up “the shared pool of freely available knowledge and creative work on the internet.”

articles.title: Trump tells 60 Minutes undocumented workers like landscapers and hotel maids could be allowed to stay in bipartisan deal
articles.summary: The president made the comment the same day he promoted Stephen Miller — a hard-liner in favor of sharply restricting immigration — as the White House chief...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has suggested that undocumented landscapers, hotel maids, restaurant employees and others could be allowed to stay in a bipartisan immigration deal negotiated with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

"Well, the deal would be we would work something out," Trump told "60 Minutes" on CBS News in an interview that was taped on Nov. 6 and aired Nov. 8. "And I think it's something-- I think that's something that's actually doable."

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

"When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's worked there as — you know, as a maid, as a cleaner…great jobs, and all of a sudden, they're being taken outta the country, it's tough," Trump said. "It's a tough thing."

Trump's remarks were made on the same day he promoted Stephen Miller , a hard-liner in favor of sharply restricting immigration, to the White House chief of staff post. Democratic leaders quickly bashed the promotion , with one calling for Miller to be fired.

The president, though, has issued mixed signals on immigration since the interview aired. He later affirmed his support for an immigration policy that doesn't confer legal status on people residing in the U.S. without authorization. "We have a very strong deportation policy. There's no amnesty," he said at a Nov. 9 press conference . "We keep that, but we focus on the worst of the worst."

In the "60 Minutes" interview, Trump credited his hard-line immigration policy for bolstering support, but admitted it also dissuaded some voters from backing the Republicans in the midterms.

"I think it both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," he said. "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."

He also cracked the door open to a deal for unauthorized immigrants, particularly for those who have been paying federal income and payroll taxes, as a large share already do.

"There's a large part of the country that think they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel or doing something," Trump said. "And in some cases, paying taxes."

articles.title: Nvidia is reportedly preparing to fire Jensen Huang
articles.summary: After a New York Times report that Jensen Huang had an affair with another Nvidia executive, now there’s a rumor the board will fire him.
articles.body: Nvidia’s board is preparing to dismiss CEO Jensen Huang following a report from the New York Times about a second alleged extramarital affair, just days after he admitted to a separate affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, The Wall Street Journal reports. The second alleged affair was with an executive who reports to him, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell, according to the Times. The Nvidia board will meet as soon as today to decide on Huang’s future at the company, according to the Journal. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge. Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were allegedly captured together at a hotel in San Jose during Nvidia’s GTC developer conference in March, two unnamed sources told the Times. The Times has not seen the video. Rumors about a potential affair between the two had long circulated at Nvidia, an unnamed source told CNBC, partially because Powell does not have a health or science background. Nvidia’s stock fell more than 7 percent in after-hours trading Wednesday. Since Nvidia and Huang confirmed an extramarital relationship with Megaspeed executive and alleged spy Alice Huang and a subsequent investigation over the weekend, the company has said it retained former US attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to handle it, but today’s rumor suggests it won’t wait for those results to act. Last year, Huang hired crisis communications firm Heller known for handling public sex scandals, according to Wired. Its founder has advised several powerful men who faced public scrutiny, Wired reported, like former congressman Anthony Weiner and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge.

articles.title: Trump Plans to Sell Public Land, Reducing Size of Federal Estate
articles.summary: The Trump administration has formally said it plans to sell public lands as part of a plan to reduce the size of the federal estate.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The Trump administration has formally said it plans to sell public lands as part of a plan to reduce the size of the federal estate.

The Interior Department's four-year strategic plan released on Wednesday didn't specify how much land it plans to sell or how the land would be priced. The department, which manages some 480 million acres, didn't immediately respond to a request for more details.

"The Department will work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands," the agency said in the document. "Through these sales, the Department will be able to focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands."

The Interior Department alongside the Department of Housing and Urban Development has previously called for building housing on "underutilized" federal land. But the inclusion of the land sales marks the first time the agency has officially confirmed it wants to sell federal land, said Jayson O'Neill, a spokesman for Save Our Parks, a watchdog group. He pointed out Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has previously said selling public land wasn't part of the Trump administration's agenda.

"Doug Burgum just said the quiet part out loud, confirming that the Trump administration will work to sell off America's shared public lands," O'Neill said in an email.

Burgum, a former technology executive who served as North Dakota's governor, has often talked about viewing the nation's vast federal lands, and the oil, gas, and minerals contained within, as part of "America's balance sheet," worth trillions of dollars.

Congressional condemnation of the plan was swift. Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich, who is poised to lead the Senate energy committee next year, said he would oppose efforts to sell or privatize public lands.

"These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in," Heinrich said in a statement. "Public lands belong in public hands."

articles.title: Despite Trump administration’s efforts to limit tariff refunds, American importers are one step closer to receiving $166 billion in universal rebates
articles.summary: Class counsel in Freestyle World, Inc. v. United States filed a relief motion that would automatically return money collected from the levies to all eligible...
articles.body:
U.S. importers could be one step closer to automatically receiving all of the $166 billion in tariff refunds following the Supreme Court's ruling against the levies imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).

Class counsel in a tariff refund class action against the Trump administration filed a motion in the U.S. Court of International Trade to enter a relief order on Tuesday, which would return money collected from the tariffs to the more than 330,000 importers of record, whether or not they filed an individual lawsuit against the administration. The Trump administration is fighting for only importers who sued for the refunds to receive them.

"The proposed order would give the agency the authority it says it needs to provide full refunds with interest to all class members, including the tens of thousands of small businesses who lack the resources to bring their own cases," class counsel co-leads Lawrence Friedman, partner at Barnes, Richardson & Colburn; and Elizabeth Cabraser and Nicholas Diamand, partners at Lieff Cabraser Heimann & Bernstein; told Fortune in a statement. "We will continue working closely with the Court and the government to make sure all importers who paid these unlawful tariffs receive the refunds they are owed as quickly as possible."

Tariffs became a flashpoint in the ongoing affordability crisis, which cost Republicans in the midterm elections, and refunds would not only relieve financial pressures on companies that have raised prices to offset inflation from the import taxes and the Iran war, but also increase the likelihood of American consumers seeing their own refunds in the form of payments from companies.

The Supreme Court's February ruling that tariffs imposed under IEEPA exceeded the president's powers, paved the way for hundreds of billions of dollars in tariff refunds to U.S. importers who footed the bill for the levies. While more than $115 billion have been disbursed back to American companies as of August through Customs and Border Protection's Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries (CAPE) system, thousands of importers—such as small businesses and individuals who purchased tariffed items online—have yet to receive their money back. They've encountered technical errors in their CAPE submissions, lack the legal resources of larger importers and did not submit appropriate paperwork, or went through a larger third-party importer of record.

This class action, Freestyle World, Inc. v. United States , aims to open up a pathway for these importers to receive tariff refunds without having to file individual lawsuits, which thousands of companies have already done. The case is being heard in the U.S. Court of International Trade and was certified as a class action on Oct. 8.

articles.title: FEMA tells states to prepare for a smaller federal role in disasters
articles.summary: The Trump administration appears to be gearing up for the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to provide less assistance to states — but it’s not entirely clear what will change. Michael Coen, who was the agency’s chief of staff during the Biden administration, told The Hill that during a recent emergency management conference, FEMA’s administrator…
articles.body:
The Trump administration appears to be gearing up for the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to provide less assistance to states — but it’s not entirely clear what will change.

Michael Coen, who was the agency’s chief of staff during the Biden administration, told The Hill that during a recent emergency management conference, FEMA’s administrator Cameron Hamilton “talked about the need for states to take more responsibility and to start planning for less federal support.”

“In a Q&A session, he said within six months,” Coen added.

According to Coen, Hamilton did not share details about what exactly would change within six months or how much less money the agency could dole out.

The former official said the agency is not giving states enough information or time to adequately plan for major changes.

“Some states actually spoke up at some of the breakout sessions and said that they need more time,” Coen said. “They need more definitive information so that they can inform their governor’s office and they can work with their state legislature to plan.”

Asked about what was changing, a FEMA spokesperson pointed to mitigation funding, which is used to prevent impacts from future disasters.

“Mitigation investments only achieve their purpose when they move from state accounts to communities. As a result, the administration is aligning hazard mitigation approvals not only with states’ ability to execute funds, but with ensuring state mitigation plans and project pipelines reflect the true mission and statutory intent of these programs so that dollars translate into real, measurable resilience,” the spokesperson said in an email.

The agency’s spokesperson did not provide additional details, but said that in general, “federal assistance is meant to support state and local response, not to replace it, and cannot make individuals or communities whole after a disaster.”

“While FEMA supplements local efforts where needed through federal support, FEMA’s primary focus is on empowering communities to lead and execute disaster response and recovery,” the spokesperson, who did not provide their name and responded from a generic press inbox, continued.

Politico first reported, based on a recording it obtained , that Hamilton told attendees at last month’s National Emergency Management Association conference that “every state must have the appropriate financial reserves” so they can “ensure that recovery efforts can start immediately and not necessarily be held up simply because of the federal [disaster] declaration process.”

The news outlet quoted him as saying he hoped for a future with fewer federal disaster declarations “because the capability of states is so high and so substantial.” Hamilton was also quoted as saying that changes could start “in the next six months” and describing a “national mutual aid” system where states would help each other.

This is not the first time in the Trump administration that FEMA has indicated it would like to scale back assistance to states. President Trump has been putting that message forward for more than a year after his administration moved away from calls to eliminate the disaster assistance agency outright.

However, the six-month time frame appears to be new.

Jay Inslee, the former Democratic governor of Washington, told The Hill that that’s not enough time.

“You can’t budget something for just six months from now. If they’re going to do this, they need to give state and local communities years to readjust their entire financial plans,” he said.

He added that cutting federal funding is “going to mean less school for kids or more taxes for taxpayers locally, or the death of these communities that can never be rebuilt, and to spring this on local communities is just vindictive.”

Inslee said that Washington has “biannual budget, so it takes you two years to even plan.”

Karen Langdon, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Association, said via email that the organization, made up of state and territory emergency management directors, “supports changes that expedite disaster assistance to impacted communities and individuals, but it’s important to recognize that state-level legislation may be required for new appropriations, staffing, and other resources to take on greater responsibility.”

“Some states may require multiple legislative cycles due to biennial legislatures to authorize and fund implementation,” Langdon said, adding that Hamilton “stressed the need to reduce risk and build capability at the state and local level” but that “no specific timelines were officially announced.”

Annie Mack Vest, who recently departed from her role as executive director at the Oklahoma Department of Emergency Management, told The Hill in October she does think states could adjust to changes at FEMA but said they need to know what is changing and be able to provide input.

“The states should know and the state should be able to provide feedback,” said Vest, who was with the state at the time of interview. “I want FEMA to get it right, and I’m hopeful that they’re taking that time to do so, and that means getting good feedback from the states.”

Vest said, however, that her state has been working to be more self-sufficient.

She said that after Oklahoma was hit with bad tornadoes in spring 2024 the state started “a resilient recovery strategy” that included integrated planning that leveraged the scope of 32,000 state employees, not just those working in emergency management.

She said state agencies have also worked with local governments and community- and faith-based organizations, and she thinks other states can make changes to bolster their own capabilities.

“We have a tremendous amount of expertise across this nation in state emergency management directors and then also the technical discipline, so I think now is the time for emergency management to think much broader to who needs to be at that table and if we can bring more people to the table to be part of that solution, I think it is replicable nationwide,” Vest said.

Vest added that while Hamilton did not detail what changes were coming, the “tone” of the changes was about “making things simple and really building the capacity of state governments.”

“I feel really confident in the regional administrators that he’s put in place across the country,” she said. “That message is really clear that FEMA is here with us and for us and planning with us. I think what time will tell is how much financial resource comes with that. But these programs need to be simplified, and I think states are eager to take on more responsibility as long as there’s also still financial resource that comes with that when we need it.”

Meanwhile, Brian Sigritz, director of state fiscal studies at the National Association of State Budget Officers, said that less money from FEMA could exacerbate existing strains on state budgets.

“States are already dealing with some of these federal cost shifts, a number brought upon by One Big Beautiful Bill Act, with the two largest areas being in Medicaid and SNAP [Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program],” he said.

He said that some states, however, are already trying to prepare for less federal disaster funding.

“We’ve already seen efforts by states to increase disaster funding in recent years. We’ve seen some states create new separate disaster funds, and we’ve also seen more funding put aside for different resiliency efforts,” Sigritz said. “But there’s, you know, there’s a lot of questions right now on both timing and the exact structure of proposed federal changes.”

articles.title: Hegseth survives the battle. Democrats aren’t done with the war
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth survived another battle with Democrats when House Republicans this week sent back eight articles of impeachment brought by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.). While Massie won’t be back next year, Democrats are not done with the Defense secretary, who remains a key target for scrutiny — and possibly another impeachment vote —…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth survived another battle with Democrats when House Republicans this week sent back eight articles of impeachment brought by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.).

While Massie won’t be back next year, Democrats are not done with the Defense secretary, who remains a key target for scrutiny — and possibly another impeachment vote — once they are in the majority next year.

But for now, Hegseth, a former Army National Guard major, has some breathing room and a close ally in Stephen Miller, who is taking over as chief of staff at the White House.

“To quote Frederick Nietzsche: ‘What does not kill me makes me stronger.’ Tonight, Pete Hegseth is stronger than he was this afternoon and this morning, largely because of Democrat incompetence,” former Trump campaign adviser David Urban said Tuesday night on CNN, pointing to 11 House Democrats who missed the vote against a Pentagon chief they have called a threat to national security.

Following the GOP’s midterm defeats, where they lost control of the House and Senate in the next Congress, some Hegseth critics within the administration blamed him for pushing Trump into a war against Iran, a conflict that contributed to the election drubbing.

Trump was asking allies and advisers last week about Hegseth’s standing, The Hill previously reported . But the president publicly stood by the Defense secretary, praising him for doing a “great job” in getting rid of “woke” generals.

He again praised Hegseth on Wednesday during the Veterans Day observance at Arlington National Cemetery, prompting applause and cheering among the crowd.

“I had a feeling that was going to happen,” Trump said of the reaction. “He’s done a fantastic job and he loves you and protects you. He’s all about you.”

House Democrats appear somewhat divided over how to handle Hegseth moving forward. Some are pushing leadership to bring impeachment articles against the Defense secretary, who they argue is unqualified for the role. Others are more cautious.

“As Secretary of Defense, he has made America less safe through his chaos and gross incompetence. Republicans’ refusal to stand up for our Constitution and the rule of law is disgusting,” Rep. Betty McCollum (D-Minn.), top Democrat of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, said in a statement late Tuesday.

“When Democrats take the majority in the 120th Congress, we will hold Secretary Hegseth accountable for his illegal actions.”

“We need to take a long, hard look at what makes sense,” Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.), the incoming House Armed Services Committee chair, said Wednesday, according to Punchbowl News. “I think Hegseth has committed impeachable offenses. I think he should be removed, [but] what’s our best approach to achieve our broader objectives?”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has signaled that Smith would be one of the leaders in charge of any Hegseth impeachment proceedings next year.

The president’s decision to remove Susie Wiles and install Miller as White House chief of staff likely bodes well for Hegseth in the months ahead.

Miller is seen as one of Hegseth’s allies in the White House, and the two have a “very good” and “close” relationship, according to four sources familiar with the dynamics.

“This couldn’t be any better” for Hegseth, one U.S. official told The Hill regarding Miller’s appointment as chief of staff.

The two live on the same military base and their wives, Katie Miller and Jennifer Hegseth, are friends. And they are on the same page when it comes to U.S. policy on Latin America, according to a senior Pentagon official.

A senior administration official said Hegseth and Miller have been “extremely close” since the start of Trump’s second term, and their partnership has been “instrumental” in helping secure the U.S.-Mexico border, deploying National Guard troops to American cities and in the U.S. military lethal campaign against alleged drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.

“The speed and effectiveness of this all getting done were unprecedented,” the senior administration official said. “And I think you’ll continue to see how lockstep they are in the coming months and not just with the president’s priorities.”

Hegseth has called Miller an “incredible American patriot and a great friend” of the Pentagon after his promotion.

“The Department of War has no better friend and advocate than Stephen Miller,” the Defense secretary said in a statement to The Hill, using the administration’s preferred name for the Department of Defense.

Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), a Hegseth ally who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, said he wasn’t sure if Democrats would make another run at impeaching Hegseth.

“Secretary Hegseth is a warrior. He served himself in uniform, and he understands what it is to be a true leader. And that, in many cases, will intimidate Democrats,” said Mills, who lost his reelection race, in a phone interview with The Hill on Wednesday.

“And so will this be the last time that they try and make such an attempt with the large majority they will come in to the House at the 120th [Congress] or with their majority in the Senate? I’m not so sure.”

Hegseth and his aides ridiculed Massie’s impeachment salvo in the lead-up to the vote. And his team is likely to repeat the tactic if Democrats try to impeach the defense secretary once they regain majorities in January.

If the House does send impeachment articles to the Senate in the next Congress, Democrats would need to peel off a few Republicans in the upper chamber for a conviction.

The White House said Tuesday night’s vote was a “massive victory” and that Trump and his team will not allow Democrats and “disgruntled” members of Congress to “ smear and demean an American patriot” like Hegseth.

articles.title: Ring confirms its camera drone won’t have manual controls after crashing on CBS News
articles.summary: When (or if) Ring’s security camera drone flies into our homes in January, you won’t get the option to pilot it yourself.﻿
articles.body: When (or if) Ring’s security camera drone flies into our homes in January, you won’t get the option to pilot it yourself. The Ring Drone Cam relies entirely on an “AI Pilot” system to follow pre-programmed routes and navigate autonomously around obstacles, with no manual control option available — and an embarrassing demonstration with CBS News might reveal why. The video, broadcast on CBS Mornings and published on Threads, shows Ring founder Jamie Siminoff allowing technology reporter Jo Ling Kent to manually fly an early version of the drone via a mobile app with integrated controls. > Ling Kent: “Can I control it?” > Siminoff: “Yeah, so we can load manual controls.” The demo then shows the drone crashing twice while being manually piloted. In the first instance, Ring reportedly told CBS News that the drone’s collision avoidance technology malfunctioned, and declined to share the video recorded by the drone prior to crashing. CBS News caught the second crash on camera, with the footage showing the drone colliding with a wall after failing to respond to manual controls. According to Siminoff, this occurred because the drone lost internet connectivity — which it also relies on to fly autonomously. [Media: “If it loses connectivity, it’s supposed to stop and land,” Siminoff said in the video. “It did not there.” Ring declined to show us the app in our own demonstration of the Drone Cam, and said it only works on pre-programmed flight paths. It seems that while manual flight controls were included at some stage of development, Ring won’t be making the feature available to customers when the Drone Cam launches in January. “We explored a lot of features throughout the development, but autonomous flight to patrol points using the AI Pilot is the best customer benefit and experience,” Ring spokesperson Sam McGee said in a statement to The Verge. Ring didn’t respond to our question regarding whether the decision to not include manual controls was made following the CBS News demo.

articles.title: 5 myths about data broker opt-outs that expose retirees
articles.summary: Data broker opt-outs may not keep your personal information private for long. Five common myths leave retirees especially vulnerable to scams.
articles.body: Have you already tried removing your personal information from data broker sites? If so, you might have Googled your name, disliked what you saw and spent an afternoon filling out opt-out forms on sites like Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified. That took real effort, and it wasn't wasted. Unfortunately, completing a few data broker opt-outs doesn't necessarily mean your information will stay private. It comes down to how data brokers operate. Their practices can be confusing, and some common misconceptions leave people exposed without realizing it. For retirees, the stakes can be especially high. Decades of public records, property ownership history and family connections can give scammers plenty of information to work with. I've spent years covering how scammers operate. And here's something I've noticed. Sometimes, people take reasonable steps to protect themselves, then assume the problem has been solved. That's where trouble can begin. Let's clear up five myths about data broker opt-outs that could put your privacy and financial security at risk. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES Myth 1: "I already opted out, so my data is gone" This may be the most dangerous misconception, especially for retirees who've already taken steps to protect their privacy. Here's the reality. Hundreds of data brokers operate in the United States. When you submit an opt-out request to Spokeo, you've addressed your information on that particular service. What about everyone else? Other data brokers may still have your name, home address, phone number and information about your relatives. Some also compile estimates about your finances and property. And even the site you opted out of could eventually list your information again. According to the Federal Trade Commission, information can reappear on people-search websites when the underlying public records change. Those records may include property filings and other government documents that remain publicly accessible. That's why one round of data broker opt-outs may only provide temporary relief. Myth 2: "My family's personal information doesn't affect me" This one concerns me because it involves the people closest to us. Data broker profiles frequently include information about relatives and household members. That means your information could still appear in someone else's listing even after you've removed your own profile. Let's say your daughter completes several opt-outs. Her personal listing disappears from those sites. However, your profile could still identify her as a relative and reveal details about where she lives. Now consider what happens when a scammer uses that information to research your family. Your phone rings. "Grandpa, it's me. I'm in the hospital. Please don't tell Mom. She'll worry. Can you wire me $1,200?" The caller knows your granddaughter's name and how you're related. Those details can make the emergency sound believable. And with AI voice cloning, criminals may even imitate a loved one's voice if they have access to a suitable audio sample. This type of fraud is commonly called the grandparent scam. The consequences can be devastating. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, people 60 and older filed more than 201,000 complaints involving over $7.7 billion in reported losses. The average reported loss was approximately $38,500 per complaint. Those figures cover internet crime reported by older adults, not grandparent scams alone. Still, they show the financial danger facing this age group. A family code word and a rule to call relatives back using a trusted number can help stop these scams before money changes hands. Myth 3: "My information isn't interesting enough to target" I understand why this feels true. You're probably not a celebrity. You may not post much on social media. Perhaps you've lived a relatively private life. Why would a scammer care about you? Here's what someone searching data broker websites might discover: DATA BROKERS DON'T JUST COLLECT FACTS. THEY GUESS ABOUT YOU The amount and accuracy of this information vary by broker. However, criminals can combine publicly available details with information from other sources to build a more convincing profile. Think about how many companies still ask questions about your previous addresses or family history when verifying your identity. Suddenly, those old records become more valuable to someone trying to impersonate you. And the concern goes beyond theory. A 2025 analysis of FBI data estimated that access to personal information online could have contributed to 72% of reported internet-crime incidents involving older Americans in 2024. However, that figure is based on an assessment of crime categories and does not prove that data brokers played a role in every case. Still, the findings highlight how exposed personal details can help criminals carry out scams. Retirees may be especially attractive targets because scammers often assume they've accumulated savings or valuable property. The less personal information criminals can easily find, the harder it becomes for them to create convincing, personalized scams. Myth 4: "If I haven't been targeted yet, I must be safe" Here's another way to think about that. You may have received a suspicious email that landed in your spam folder. Perhaps someone called pretending to represent your bank, but you hung up. Or maybe you got a strange text message and deleted it without responding. Any of those situations sound familiar? Scammers attempt to reach people every day. However, you may never know whether a particular attempt used information from a data broker. Meanwhile, your personal details could remain available online. Some data brokers continually update their databases as new information becomes available. As a result, previously removed information may eventually reappear. And there's evidence that personal data has been deliberately supplied to criminals. In September 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice announced prison sentences for two former Epsilon employees involved in selling targeted consumer lists to fraudsters. According to prosecutors, those lists helped criminals target older and vulnerable Americans through fraudulent mail campaigns. In one scheme, the criminals defrauded more than 218,000 victims out of over $23.7 million. That's a sobering example of how personal information can become a tool for financial crime. If you're retired and have spent decades building your savings, protecting information about your household deserves serious attention. Waiting until something goes wrong could prove expensive. Myth 5: "This is a technology problem for younger people" Maybe your grandchildren grew up with smartphones and social media. You didn't. So it's tempting to think online privacy concerns belong to younger generations. But data brokers don't need you to have an Instagram account to collect information about your life. Think about the records you've accumulated over the years. Perhaps you bought your first home in 1978. That property transaction may still appear in public records. You might also have records associated with: Some of this information can be legally obtained through public records and other databases. And although the amount of information varies, data brokers can combine records from different sources to create detailed profiles. Your grandchildren may have more social media activity. However, you could have a much longer public record history. That's worth remembering the next time someone suggests online privacy is only a concern for younger people. DATA BROKER OPT-OUT: HOW RETIREES CAN PROTECT THEIR DATA How to make data broker opt-outs more effective The most practical approach involves regular checks and repeated removal requests. You can do this yourself by searching data broker websites, submitting opt-out forms and returning periodically to see whether your information has reappeared. The Federal Trade Commission confirms that manual opt-outs are free, although the process can take time. And with hundreds of data brokers collecting personal information, keeping track of every website can feel overwhelming. Another option is to use a personal data removal service. These services can automate opt-out requests across multiple data broker websites and continue checking for information that reappears. Some also offer family plans, which may be helpful for retirees whose personal information is connected to adult children or other relatives. However, no service can remove every piece of information from the internet. Public records and information held outside participating databases may remain accessible. The goal is to reduce how much personal information scammers can easily find about you. Whether you handle removals yourself or use an automated service, staying consistent is one of the best ways to help protect your privacy. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com. Kurt's key takeaways Here's what concerns me most. You can spend hours removing your personal information from data broker websites and still have details about your life floating around online. That's frustrating, especially when you've already made the effort to protect yourself. And for retirees, decades of public records can give scammers information they may use to make a convincing phone call or attempt to steal your identity. Your family's information can also lead criminals right back to you. That's why I believe ongoing data removal deserves a place in your privacy routine. A data removal service can help make that process easier, although no service can guarantee everything will disappear. My advice? Don't assume one round of opt-outs means you're finished. Keep checking, talk to your family about protecting their information and remember that a scammer who knows personal details about you could still be a complete stranger. Have you ever searched your name online and been shocked by how much personal information was available? What worries you more, strangers knowing where you live or having access to details about your children and grandchildren? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com. articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid affair scandals
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will step down from his role at the AI chip giant following explosive reports of two extramarital affairs, one of which involved an alleged Chinese spy. The company announced Thursday morning that Huang was resigning immediately and Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia, will take over…
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will step down from his role at the AI chip giant following explosive reports of two extramarital affairs, one of which involved an alleged Chinese spy.

The company announced Thursday morning that Huang was resigning immediately and Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia, will take over as interim CEO.

“Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the company wrote in a press release Thursday.

The embattled tech leader admitted Sunday to having an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. officials concluded was passing information to Beijing, sparking widespread national security concerns given Nvidia’s prominent role in the AI race and Huang’s close relationship with President Trump.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a separate affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

Huang’s resignation is likely to send ripple effects throughout Silicon Valley and Wall Street. Nvidia, under Huang’s leadership, has become an AI powerhouse, providing the advanced chips underpinning the technology’s development.

The company’s stock tanked as markets opened Thursday morning following the news, dropping more than 10 points.

The revelations about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an executive with the data center and cloud computing firm Megaspeed, sparked quick scrutiny on Capitol Hill. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle called for investigations into whether Jensen Huang compromised national security and reiterated calls to pass chip export control bills.

U.S. officials concluded Alice Huang was recruited by China to pass along information.

Kress has worked at Nvidia since 2013, leading the tech giant’s finance organization, the company said. She spent more than two decades at other tech giants like Microsoft and Cisco.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chair of the board, said in a statement.

The company’s board said it is initiating a search for a permanent replacement, with both internal and external candidates up for consideration.

In an internal message sent to staff, Kress wrote, “I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy.”

“The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication,” Kress wrote in the message, obtained by The Hill. “Thank you.”

“We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let’s move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company,” Kress said.

Jensen Huang is one of Trump’s fiercest allies in the technology industry. The president stood behind Huang in the immediate aftermath of the scandal earlier this week, calling the technology executive an “honorable guy.”

“I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job and so I would certainly hope he’s a fine person, in my opinion,” he added.

The president on Monday said Huang told him he was not aware the Megaspeed executive was an intelligence operative for Beijing.

The Times first reported last month that Trump was briefed about a year ago that the U.S. intelligence community believed Alice Huang was an operative for China’s government.

The president didn’t do anything with the information at the time, according to the newspaper.

It marks a moment of upheaval for the company. Jensen Huang has led Nvidia since he helped found the chipmaker in the early 1990s. What started as a relatively obscure company making chips for video games became a behemoth in the new AI era.

The release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in late 2022 kicked off an AI boom that put the company’s chips , known as graphics processing units, in high demand. In early 2023, Nvidia was valued at less than $1 trillion, but by late 2025, it was the world’s first $5 trillion company.

As it became increasingly crucial to AI development, Nvidia found itself navigating a complex and often tenuous relationship between the U.S. and China — two superpowers who are competing for dominance on the technology.

Washington has placed increasingly strict export controls on Nvidia’s chips in an effort to curb China’s access and, in turn, development of AI.

Huang has advocated in D.C. for fewer restrictions on chip sales, arguing that allowing the company’s third- or fourth-best chips to reach China can keep the country’s AI industry dependent on American-made infrastructure.

The Nvidia chief saw some key successes. The Trump administration allowed for sales of the company’s H20 and H200 chips to China last year.

Nvidia will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results next Tuesday, with its earnings call to follow.
