articles.title: Cop fired over fake Facebook page targeting mom
articles.summary: Natasha Lopez says a Flock camera system helped a Georgia deputy track her family, and after she spoke out, a fake Facebook page targeted her children.
articles.body: You come home with your kids after an afternoon at a trampoline park. A sheriff's deputy is waiting outside. He's investigating your adult son and later demands that everyone leave your house. You ask whether he has a search warrant. Minutes later, you're being arrested while your terrified children watch. That's how Georgia mom Natasha Lopez describes the police encounter that changed her family's life. But what happened afterward took an even more disturbing turn. In my conversation with Natasha on The CyberGuy Report podcast, she described how a Flock license plate camera system allegedly helped a deputy track someone to her home. After Natasha publicly challenged her arrest, a fake Facebook page began attacking her family. The page allegedly shared sensitive records involving her children and AI-generated images designed to humiliate her. The deputy who arrested her has since been fired. In a statement provided to CyberGuy, the Cherokee County Sheriff's Office confirmed that its investigation found him responsible for the Facebook page's content. However, the department strongly disputes Natasha's account of the original arrest and how authorities handled her complaints. Now, with a protective order in place and her criminal case still unresolved, Natasha says her family continues to live with the consequences. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. YOUR BUMPER STICKER COULD HELP FLOCK CAMERAS TRACK WHERE YOU GO — NEW BILL AIMS TO STOP IT How Flock cameras allegedly led police to Natasha's home The trouble began on August 30, 2025, when Cherokee County Sheriff's Corporal Charles Mills was investigating Natasha's adult son. Authorities suspected him of fleeing police on a motorcycle during an earlier encounter. According to Natasha, Mills used Flock automated license plate readers to follow the movements of her son's girlfriend as she traveled to Natasha's house. "He was investigating my adult son, who he alleged was speeding on a motorcycle the night before," Natasha told me. Flock cameras capture passing vehicles and record license plates along with their location and time. Police can search those records to identify where a vehicle appeared. Multiple camera sightings can reveal someone's movements across an area. Natasha believes those camera searches led Mills to her home. When Natasha returned from the trampoline park with her younger children, deputies were already at her home. Natasha questions how Mills connected her son to the motorcycle involved in the alleged incident. She says Mills relied on a Flock camera image captured approximately six hours before the reported encounter and at a different location. She believes that evidence did not establish that her son was the rider. She asked for a warrant and ended up arrested Mills had an arrest warrant for Natasha's adult son. However, authorities had not yet obtained a search warrant for Natasha's home. After taking her son into custody, the deputy demanded that everyone leave the house. Natasha wanted to know why he needed to enter. "Do you have a warrant?" she recalled asking. She says she repeatedly requested documentation authorizing a search. Instead, Mills walked past her and entered the house. "And I remember saying, like, my kids and my dogs are in there, like, what are you doing?" Natasha told me. She followed him inside because her children were there. At the same time, she called 911 because she believed the deputy had entered without proper authorization. Her home surveillance cameras captured the confrontation. Natasha says she never expected an argument over a warrant to end with her being placed in handcuffs. "I felt very helpless, very scared, very scared for my children because they were taking the only parent that they had," she said. What the sheriff's office says about the arrest The Cherokee County Sheriff's Office disputes Natasha's characterization of the encounter. In a statement provided to CyberGuy, the department said Mills believed evidence connected to the felony traffic investigation was inside the home. According to the agency, he attempted to conduct a protective sweep to clear individuals from the residence and preserve potential evidence before obtaining a search warrant. The department maintains that Mills believed his actions were permitted under established Fourth Amendment case law. It also says Natasha interfered with his efforts despite repeated lawful orders. The sheriff's office emphasized that Mills was wearing his full uniform, operating a marked patrol vehicle and had identified himself as a law enforcement officer. After securing the residence, Mills obtained a search warrant from a judge. Natasha was transported to the Cherokee County Adult Detention Center, processed and later released on bond. Authorities charged her with obstruction of a law enforcement officer under Georgia law. The sheriff's office also told CyberGuy that prosecutors independently reviewed body-camera footage and determined there was probable cause to pursue the case. An additional obstruction charge was subsequently filed. Natasha maintains that she was exercising her rights and trying to protect her children. Her attorneys have challenged the legal basis for the deputy's actions. The court would later address those arguments, but the encounter had already set off another chain of events. Why Natasha took her story to social media After leaving jail, Natasha began asking questions about what happened. She told me she had asked supervising deputies to review her home security footage before taking her into custody. She believed the recording would show that the arresting deputy had misrepresented the encounter. "I told them the arresting officer wasn't telling the truth, and they would not," she said, referring to her requests that officials review the footage. After her release, Natasha says she contacted the sheriff's office and prosecutors. She hoped someone would investigate her complaint. Instead, she felt that authorities had dismissed her concerns. She eventually began sharing her experience publicly through a social media page called Natasha Noble. She wanted people in her community to see what happened and decide for themselves. The sheriff's office offered a different perspective on the social media activity that followed. In its response to CyberGuy, the department described Natasha's posts as an online campaign targeting Mills, other deputies, elected officials, prosecutors and their families. It also said employees and their families had received hateful messages and death threats from individuals across the country. The department reported that its phone lines had been inundated with disturbing calls and said the attention surrounding the case had adversely affected employees and their families. Its statement did not establish that Natasha personally made those threats. Meanwhile, Natasha's public criticism of her arrest was followed by another problem. A fake Facebook page starts attacking Natasha's family Natasha noticed an anonymous Facebook page while checking reactions to one of her posts. The account was called Not So Noble, a play on the name of her own page. It used her branding and published material criticizing her. At first, she did not know who was behind it. Then the posts became increasingly personal. "It was a like, harassment page that somebody had made, that they were attacking me and my children on," she told me. Natasha says the page accused her children of criminal behavior and published personal information about them. Some posts allegedly included unredacted school and incident reports involving minors. That frightened her because she could not understand how the person behind the page was obtaining those records. She also noticed people connected to local law enforcement interacting with the content. However, she had no proof at that point of who controlled the page. As the posts continued, her concern shifted toward her children's safety. "I felt desperate, like, how, how how do I protect my children, you know?" she said. Natasha told me she filed a complaint with the sheriff's department because she feared for her family's safety. She says she wanted investigators to identify the person behind the page but felt authorities were unwilling to help. TENNESSEE COPS RAIDED MAN'S HOME AFTER HE CRITICIZED OFFICER FOR SPEEDING: LAWSUIT What the sheriff's office says about Natasha's complaint The Cherokee County Sheriff's Office disputes Natasha's description of how investigators handled her report. In its response to CyberGuy, the department said Natasha filed a complaint concerning Not So Noble in June 2026. According to the agency, she initially suggested that a woman known to her might have created the page and provided screenshots for investigators to review. The department said detectives did not believe the screenshots established criminal conduct at that time. However, investigators identified reported telephone calls that could potentially violate Georgia's harassing telephone call statute. According to the sheriff's office, detectives asked Natasha to come in for a formal interview and possible additional evidence collection. The department says she did not communicate with investigators for approximately one week and later advised that she was unavailable to meet with the assigned detective. The agency maintains that the investigation could not move forward without her participation. Natasha disputes how authorities handled her requests for assistance. During our podcast conversation, she described feeling abandoned while the online targeting escalated. Then came the AI-generated intimate images The online targeting eventually took an especially disturbing turn. According to Natasha, the Facebook page began posting personal photographs of her and digitally manipulated images designed to make her appear connected to an OnlyFans account. Some photographs were years old. Natasha says she still does not know how the original images were obtained. "I don't know, we still don't know," she told me when I asked where the photographs came from. The images allegedly included AI-generated material created using her likeness. Natasha says the posts also directed people to folders on Google Drive, where copies of the images and other material could be viewed. She repeatedly reported the content to Facebook and Google. Although some images were removed, she says additional versions continued appearing online. What upset her most was the apparent effort to expose her children to the material. "They wanted, like, my children to see it," Natasha said. For Natasha, the situation became especially frightening because she still did not know who was responsible. We reached out to Meta, Facebook's parent company, for comment on the page and Natasha's reports of harassment. A Meta representative told CyberGuy that the account appears to have already been removed. The deputy who arrested her was behind the Facebook page The biggest revelation came during a September 18, 2026 court hearing. Natasha says her attorney questioned Mills about records he had obtained involving her. Then the attorney asked whether he had created fake social media accounts. Mills acknowledged using fake Facebook profiles to monitor Natasha's posts after she blocked him. That admission did not immediately establish that he operated Not So Noble. However, prosecutors subsequently disclosed that Mills was the page's creator and owner. When I asked Natasha how she reacted to learning that the arresting officer was connected to the page, she struggled to describe the shock. "Disgust. Anger. Sadness. Fear," she said. "I couldn't believe it." Natasha says she suspected someone connected to law enforcement might be involved because of the records appearing online. But she had never expected the person responsible to be the deputy who arrested her. Mills and his wife fired as investigation continues The Cherokee County Sheriff's Office told CyberGuy that prosecutors formally notified the department on September 21, 2026, that Mills was potentially involved in the Not So Noble Facebook page. The following day, September 22, Mills was placed on administrative leave while the department opened an internal investigation. On October 2, the department terminated his employment. The sheriff's office confirmed its investigation determined that Mills was responsible for the page's content and that his actions violated department policy. In its statement to CyberGuy, the department emphasized, "The personal actions of Charles Aaron Mills do not reflect the values and ethical standards of the Cherokee Sheriff's Office." Meanwhile, Cherokee Judicial Circuit District Attorney Erle Newton confirmed to CyberGuy that his office was assigned to investigate Mills' actions alongside the Georgia Bureau of Investigation. Newton said that the investigation remains ongoing and that no criminal charges had been filed at the time of his response. CyberGuy has also confirmed that Mills' wife was fired from her position at the Blue Ridge Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office on September 30, 2026. The office said her termination was based on policy violations but declined to provide further details, citing its recusal from investigations involving social media content about Natasha Lopez. It remains unclear whether her firing was connected to the allegations involving her husband. Despite those developments, important questions remain. The department's findings establish Corporal Mills' responsibility for the Facebook page's content, but they do not explain how sensitive records involving Natasha's children were obtained or who generated each allegedly manipulated image. Natasha also questioned whether other local government employees knew about the page. It's still unclear whether anyone else knew about it or helped Corporal Mills. We reached out to Mills' attorney for comment on the allegations and the sheriff's office's findings, but did not hear back before our deadline. Natasha wins a protective order, but her fight continues The deputy's termination did not bring Natasha the closure she wanted. She sought legal protection from Mills after identifying him as the person behind the Facebook page. On October 20, 2026, a Cherokee County Superior Court granted her a 12-month stalking protective order against the former deputy. Natasha told me the process had been extremely expensive. She estimated that one day of legal proceedings connected to obtaining protection cost her about $7,000. That financial burden added another source of frustration to an experience that had already taken an enormous emotional toll. During our conversation, she repeatedly questioned when the ordeal would finally end. "At what point do they stop, you know?" she asked. Judge upholds the legal basis for the home search Meanwhile, Natasha's original obstruction case remains unresolved. In an October 2026 ruling, a Cherokee County judge declined to dismiss the charges stemming from her August 2025 arrest. According to the sheriff's office, the court determined that the protective sweep and subsequent search of Natasha's residence were lawful and consistent with the Fourth Amendment. The judge found that Mills had probable cause to enter the home and that it was reasonable for him to believe urgent circumstances justified securing the property before obtaining a search warrant. The ruling allows the obstruction prosecution to continue. Natasha maintains that her arrest was unjustified. Her attorneys have challenged the deputy's actions throughout the proceedings. FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES What happened to Natasha's children? The original investigation also led to the arrest of Natasha's adult son, Joseph Christopher Helms. Natasha says Mills arrested him outside her home shortly before taking her into custody. She maintains that her son was wrongly identified as the motorcyclist suspected of fleeing police and says he continues to deny the allegation. Cherokee County court records show he was indicted on November 10, 2025, under case number 25CR1207. District Attorney Erle Newton told CyberGuy that the Blue Ridge Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office recused itself from Helms' case. Newton said the Prosecuting Attorneys' Council informed him that the case had been assigned to the Paulding Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office. Paulding Judicial Circuit District Attorney Robert S. Lane subsequently confirmed to CyberGuy that his office has been appointed to handle the case. Helms faces two counts of fleeing or attempting to elude a police officer. Lane said the case remains pending and no trial or hearing had been scheduled at the time of his response. Helms has not been convicted of those charges. But what stayed with me most from our conversation was what Natasha shared about her youngest son. He was 9 when deputies entered their home and arrested his mother. She says he has needed therapy since the encounter and still fears police will take her away again. "You know, we go somewhere and he'll ask me like, mom, are they going to take you?" she told me. Natasha says her son was hyperventilating after officers took her away. "Nobody even asked him if he was okay," she recalled. Meanwhile, she says some of the online posts targeted her teenage son and damaged his personal relationships. For this family, the consequences extend far beyond the courtroom. Why Natasha wants Flock cameras removed The Flock camera system remains central to Natasha's concerns about the case. She believes access to vehicle location records helped Mills follow her son's girlfriend, who Natasha says was not suspected of a crime. She also questions whether existing department policies provide enough oversight to prevent officers from abusing the system. When I asked Natasha how the experience changed her opinion of Flock cameras, she told me, "We want them gone because policies aren't enough." She believes state lawmakers need to establish stronger restrictions on how police use license plate reader data. Flock cameras can provide valuable leads in criminal investigations. However, officers may have access to large amounts of vehicle movement information. Flock Safety says its systems include search logs and auditing tools to help departments monitor access. Still, those safeguards cannot prevent every potential misuse. The Cherokee County Sheriff's Office did not specifically address Mills' use of Flock cameras or whether investigators identified any violations involving the technology. We previously covered a Flock camera hit that helped send the wrong woman to jail. Prosecutors eventually dropped the charges in that case. Both cases raise questions about how police use license plate surveillance and who holds them accountable. Natasha says she would speak up all over again Toward the end of our conversation, I asked Natasha a question that had been on my mind. Knowing everything she has endured, would she have stayed quiet if she could go back and do it again? "No, it wouldn't be me," she said. Natasha told me she has never been someone who stays silent when she believes something wrong has happened. "I believe in accountability. Right is right and wrong is wrong," she said. When I asked what justice would look like for her, she had a specific answer. "Accountability. I want Charles Mills to be charged. I want him to lose his post certification so he can not be law enforcement officer and harm somebody else like this again." Post certification refers to the professional credentials required for law enforcement officers in Georgia. Losing that certification could prevent Mills from serving as an officer in the state. Natasha also wants investigators to examine whether anyone else played a role in the harassment or the release of personal records. Whether those demands lead to additional consequences remains to be seen. But Natasha says she has no intention of stopping her efforts. What you can do if someone targets you online Natasha's experience also highlights how difficult online harassment can become when someone uses fake accounts and manipulated images. If something similar happens to you, preserving the evidence early can make a difference. Keep in mind that removing something from Google Search does not necessarily delete the original material from the website hosting it. For additional guidance, see our article on protecting your family from deepfakes and online abuse. Kurt's key takeaways I understand why police use Flock cameras. If someone steals my car, I'd want investigators to have technology that could help find it. But who's making sure officers use these systems responsibly? What stayed with me most from Natasha's story was hearing that her youngest son still worries police might take his mother away again. That's heartbreaking. I appreciate the Cherokee County Sheriff's Office responding to our questions. A judge upheld the legal basis for entering Natasha's home, while the department confirmed Mills violated its policies through his involvement with the fake Facebook page. Mills was fired, and Natasha secured a protective order, but her criminal case continues. I hope the remaining questions get answered, especially how this was allowed to happen. To hear Natasha tell her story in her own words, listen to The CyberGuy Report podcast at cyberguy.com/podcast/. She shares more about what happened to her family and why she refuses to back down. Should a police officer who creates fake social media accounts to target someone they arrested ever be allowed to work in law enforcement again? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com. articles.title: Cyberattack on Fireworks AI allowed hackers to access Notion customers' chat transcripts | TechCrunch
articles.summary: This is Fireworks' second data breach in as many months.
articles.body:
A cyberattack at Fireworks AI has exposed some of its customers’ data, the company has confirmed. Fireworks AI, a platform that developers use to access and use open AI models, said an attacker breached its cloud provider to gain access to a Fireworks development system, which allowed access to some of its customers’ data.

The company said in its latest security advisory that the cybercriminals took Fireworks’ customers’ billing information and some datasets. Fireworks touts tens of thousands of customers worldwide using its platform, including legal tech company Harvey and AI company Cursor.

At least one confirmed affected customer is online document editor and notetaker Notion, which said in a disclosure that the breach affected around 1% of its own customers.

Notion said that Fireworks alerted the company to a security incident and later confirmed that the hackers had stolen some Notion customer data. On November 3, Notion said it disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleted the data stored in its systems, and stopped all connectivity between the two.

Notion confirmed this week that the hackers took chat transcripts of its Notion AI customers who used the “Insights” feature. The company said that the transcripts include “any input to or output from the model that was written to the chat,” but added that much of the data was unattributable and could not be determined from which customer it was obtained.

The breach at Fireworks AI shows how tech companies are reliant on other tech providers for their own offerings, and how cyberattacks can, as a result, spill over into other customers.

Fireworks said that it believes the hackers are financially motivated and that their goals are focused on selling tokens from breaching access to large language models, or LLMs. These schemes rely on selling to unauthorized third parties, who can burn through AI model usage without using their own resources.

This is the second breach affecting Fireworks in as many months, following a security incident in October .

articles.title: Trump calls for Tim Cook to replace Jensen Huang at Nvidia
articles.summary: President Trump suggested Thursday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should be the one to take Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s place after his exit following reports of his extramarital affairs, one of which was with an alleged Chinese spy. “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is…
articles.body:
President Trump suggested Thursday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should be the one to take Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s place after his exit following reports of his extramarital affairs , one of which was with an alleged Chinese spy.

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post Thursday.

Cook announced in April that he was stepping down as Apple CEO after 15 years of leading the company. John Ternus, who was previously a senior vice president, replaced him in the top role at the tech giant in September.

Nvidia announced earlier Thursday that Huang was resigning immediately and Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia, will take over as interim CEO.

The tech leader has been embroiled in controversy following accusations stemming from a New York Times report that claimed American authorities discovered Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang illegally smuggled advanced AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with Jensen Huang.

Following the reports, Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it would be initiating an independent investigation into the matter. The company announced Tuesday that it hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to conduct the investigation.

The board previously said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets” were compromised by Jensen Huang’s relationship with the accused Chinese spy.

The Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a separate affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, citing five people who worked at the company.

The former Nvidia CEO recently acknowledged that he has been unfaithful to his wife, adding, “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” according to a Sunday report from Bloomberg . GOP lawmakers called on him to appear in a joint, closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 to address concerns regarding Nvidia’s security protocols and his interactions with the alleged spy.

The president on Sunday called Jensen Huang an “honorable guy,” telling reporters, “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang is out. What did China want from him?
articles.summary: How the Nvidia spy scandal could backfire for Beijing, and what it tells us about AI, Trump, and export controls.
articles.body: Today, we’re talking about the Jensen Huang scandal at Nvidia, which is developing so quickly that we had to do an emergency update of this intro minutes before publishing this episode. Huang just resigned from his position as CEO of Nvidia as news of his affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, threatened to engulf the company. We’ll have more on that story as things develop and we learn how Nvidia will restructure itself after Jensen — he had something like 60 direct reports, after all, and the entire AI financial ecosystem flows through the company. This is pure Decoder bait. But just two days ago I talked to Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, about the real heart of the scandal: What would China even seek to accomplish by having a spy so close to Jensen? And what does the real state of the US-China AI conflict really looks like, particularly from the Chinese point of view? Kyle’s answers about chips and how China is perceiving the so-called AI “race” were very illuminating, but maybe even more interesting was his observation on Jensen Huang’s relationship with Trump was the most important thing of all — because maybe what China most stood to gain was someone who could whisper in the right ears. Let’s just dive right into it. But keep in mind that when we were talking, we still didn’t know what would happen with Jensen. Okay: Kyle Chan on Nvidia, China, and the future of AI export controls. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Kyle Chan, you are a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution. Welcome to Decoder. Great to be here. What on earth could we be talking about as it relates to your expertise about China today? I have a lot to ask you about Nvidia, about our relationship to China as a country, as an economy, and about national security. Let’s start at the very beginning. From all the reporting we have today, it seems like the United States government has been very worried about a company called Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy at the center of the swirling scandal around Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia. What do we know about Alice Huang and Megaspeed? We have to be careful about what we know and what we don’t know. So far, there are allegations that the US intelligence community believes that Alice Huang may be an asset of the Chinese intelligence services. Megaspeed itself is a customer of Nvidia’s and they built a data center in Malaysia. They also seem to potentially have ties with Chinese companies and could — and this is where we’re getting into what we do know and what we don’t know — potentially be a conduit for Chinese AI companies accessing cutting-edge Nvidia chips like Blackwells. --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- I want to rewind way back. The notion that the Chinese AI industry wants Nvidia chips has been floating around for years and the idea that the Chinese AI industry would somehow develop a parallel set of technology or a superior set of technology because of the constraint of not having Nvidia chips has percolated into the discourse several times. I’m particularly thinking about DeepSeek. DeepSeek launched R1 and it outperformed our models in some ways. We think they didn’t have access to the chips. There are some accusations that they had access to the chips. It turns out they did a bunch of fine-tuning on the chips they did have. What is that relationship like? Do they need the highest-end Nvidia chips? Is it true that they’re actually developing parallel technologies that might be superior to the chips they can have? Just set that stage. A lot of the details are murky, and they’re probably murky for a reason. But up until now, we saw Chinese AI companies that were very heavily dependent on Nvidia chips in order to train and run their models. In fact, they became some of the biggest contributors to the CUDA ecosystem, which is Nvidia’s software ecosystem and platform. They got very good at that, but at the same time with US export controls and greater technology restrictions on access to cutting-edge GPUs, China increasingly pushed these AI companies to switch away from Nvidia to Huawei and other domestic AI chip makers. The idea there is to develop a parallel domestic AI chip supply chain that is good enough, if not on par with, Nvidia’s latest chips, and — crucially — resilient to policy actions coming out of Washington. So that is the story up until this point. The question is, now, what is that trajectory for the Chinese GPU or AI chip development? The reason I wanted to start there is that the motivations to get close to Jensen Huang are very murky to me. As the CEO of Nvidia, I understand that everyone thinks he’s the character and he’s actually in the software designing the next generation of Nvidia GPUs, but he’s just traveling the world giving policy speeches. If you want to build a parallel GPU ecosystem, you’re trying to get close to the designers and the engineers, right? What would be the goal of trying to get close to Jensen Huang? If you wanted the design specs for the latest Nvidia GPUs, I don’t know if you would ask Jensen directly. I think you might want to go to his technical staff. He does have like 60 direct reports. Decoder is often a show about org charts and that one has been on top of my list for a long time, but we’ll set that aside for now. Keep going. What it’s really about is potentially two things. One is trying to understand, maybe to glean information about, the US policymaking process. Jensen Huang is very close to Trump. They talk a lot. Trump can apparently just call Jensen on his cell phone at any moment. In the middle of a conference. We’ve seen the video. On the other side, and maybe this is even the bigger issue, perhaps it’s the biggest concern of all, is the concern that the direction of movement could run the other way, which is that somehow through Jensen, China might be able to influence US policymaking, especially on export controls. That is the big worry from a lot of people in Washington. One of the other underlying concerns here, that I’m just trying to parse out, is that Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, is an executive at a company called Megaspeed. And through Megaspeed, Nvidia may have already been circumventing export controls. It seems like if you’re already solving the problem, maybe you should just leave it alone. How does that dynamic play out? A lot of the story is strange. Even seen in the most cynical terms, it doesn’t quite add up. There could be several different possibilities. One is that this is actually not some concerted strategy from Beijing to try to obtain chips or information or influence, but this is potentially Beijing not quite understanding the full situation and wanting to co-op this Alice Huang person and at least try to understand from her standpoint what is happening. Because I think you’re right. Already you have a very strong relationship between Nvidia and Megaspeed. You also already have — and this is on the influence side — Jensen Huang advocating for his own commercial interests, for a loosening of export controls on his own chips to China. You don’t really need Beijing to push on that gas pedal. That’s already happening. So there are some things that don’t quite make sense if you’re thinking about it from those standpoints, but if you’re thinking about it from the viewpoint of “Beijing wants visibility,” then perhaps that is another plausible explanation. Beijing just wants someone who Trump calls on the phone to advocate for their viewpoints. I see all of that, but what are we getting out of it? If the goal is Nvidia chips, it feels like that is already assured. If the goal is Nvidia engineering plans, that feels like a question mark. If the goal is influence over the Trump administration, I feel like they could have just bought cryptocurrency. [Laughs] That’s right. There’s a big swirl of what is actually happening here. Maybe your point that Beijing just needed more visibility because it is a swirl is the motivating factor. The question that leads me to is that the New York Times reports that US intelligence agencies first flagged these issues a year ago to the Trump administration. There was a memo from Marco Rubio. The reporting is that he oversaw the memo, which is as much plausible deniability as anything. He oversaw it. He was aware that there was a memo. A year ago, the United States’ national security apparatus was worried about Alice Huang at Megaspeed, her relationship with Jensen, and nothing occurred. What do you make of that? That is one of the most worrying aspects of all this. Regardless of what the details are and what is known publicly versus what our intelligence community knows, this is something that should be investigated. This is obviously a major national security issue and this is something where you don’t want someone meddling with this process. You want to do a full investigation, get to the bottom of what’s happening. I think what we’re seeing from some of the reporting is that this has been known, and in fact, if anything, there may have been efforts to try to stop this investigation or distort it in some way. That is very troubling from that internal, within-the-US-government perspective. There’s a lot going on with Nvidia in that part of the story, where Nvidia’s own spokespeople are saying, “There’s nothing going on here. This is a normal relationship,” on the record to many publications. A week later, Jensen issues his apology letter saying there was a relationship. That’s not great for John Rizzo, Nvidia’s comms person. Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, is out there saying everything is above board. Now we know not everything is above board. What do you make of Nvidia’s corporate governance here? Because there’s a whole bunch of shareholder lawsuits to come. There’s one filed as of today. I can only imagine there are more to come. Nvidia has to tread very carefully here because what you don’t want is exactly what’s already happening, which is to start to deny or dismiss some of these issues and then turn around and have to say, “Actually, there might be something there.” This is especially important now as there are growing calls for a congressional investigation. So this is going to be separate, perhaps, from within the executive branch where, again, I think we have reasons to worry about conflicts of interest and people not wanting to do this all the way. But if there’s a full-blown congressional investigation, that might reveal some things that, if you are Nvidia, you want to get out in front of rather than have to backpedal later on and explain yourself. Part of the back and forth here with the government’s concern about Alice Huang and Megaspeed is that the Commerce Department spent months looking at the company and then Teter, the general counsel of Nvidia, emailed them and invoked a direct relationship with the Commerce undersecretary, Jeff Kessler. That got the case kicked to the DOJ where everything stopped. Trump yesterday said the FBI is investigating — that’s obviously connected to the DOJ. There’s a universe where the Trump administration is trying to make this go away. Nvidia can pressure the Trump administration to make this go away. That reeks of corruption, obviously. And then you have a very empowered class of Democrats coming into Congress with polling that suggested corruption was one of the top issues in this last election. I don’t see any outcome except those Democrats and an empowered bunch of investigators and an empowered bunch of committee chairs coming after Nvidia as hard as they can. How should the company think about that? Should they just fire Jensen now to get away from it? Should they put them in front of Congress every day for the next year? How do you think that’s going to play out? I think, at the most fundamental level, they need to cooperate and comply with calls from Congress to carry out this full investigation. Because up until now, this has all been so murky, and part of the reason why this has been a stop-and-go, even though those of us in the China AI space have been hearing about this for a while. Companies like Megaspeed, their role in all this, even people like Alice Huang, have been flagged much earlier than this. The fact that this is coming out now, but also that the investigation was stopped and started within the Trump administration, is a big red flag. Ultimately, from Nvidia’s standpoint, they’re going to have to come clean with whatever Congress now requests. There are going to be a lot of hard questions from Congress, as there should be, that have been building up for some time now. If you ever looked at Jensen’s approach to chip export controls, he’s been very fiery that chip export controls are stupid. You mentioned earlier that’s in his business interest. It is better for the Chinese AI industry to be dependent on CUDA and dependent on Nvidia chips, because then if we do get into some conflict, maybe you can restrict that access and you’ll set them back. There’s some swirl of argument that he makes that says it’s in the United States’ national security interest to ship as many Nvidia GPUs to China as you can. Then there are a lot of China hawks who are saying, “Actually, you need to restrain them and keep them years behind. They will not catch up to our bleeding-edge technology. Jensen, you just keep us ahead.” It feels like, out of all of this, the China hawks are going to start winning more fights than they’re losing — arguing that the Chinese government is actively trying to impede our efforts or actively trying to influence our government. How should people think about that? What framework should we use to evaluate that mass of differing opinions, especially now that there’s a catalyst for some kind of change? I think that’s the right way to frame up this whole debate. You have, on the one hand, folks who see the US-China AI competition as a critical strategic competition and access to compute is one of the key levers there, and thus US export controls, not only as they stand now, but tightening them further will be critical to maintaining US edge in the most powerful technology of our lives. Then there are other people who are in the opposite camp who advocate for greater exports of the US AI tech stack writ large, including Nvidia chips and including to China. Up until now, that camp has been led by people like [Commerce Secretary] Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang, and Trump himself. What’s interesting is the balance of power, in terms of whose arguing gets more weight, has been shifting and will shift in light of this recent controversy. So here now those who have been advocating for more exports and fewer export controls, some of their arguments have been tainted by this process potentially, regardless of where the investigation goes. Then there’s a final variable in all this, which is China itself. That’s something that matters a lot in this discussion because in the background, China is doing two things. One, they’re trying to build their own chips and they’re sort of all-in on building a resilient semiconductor supply chain with their own, say, Huawei AI chips that their own AI companies can use. They will never really catch up. It looks highly unlikely, but they could develop good enough chips to replace the Nvidia ones that they have been dependent on for so long. The second big factor from China is retaliation. And this is one thing that I’m watching very closely. If these greater export controls are placed by the US on not just chips to China, but also on chip-making equipment — the tools required to make the semiconductors themselves — will China use its own export controls, such as restricting rare earth metals, to hit back? Right. This is in the context of an ongoing trade and tariff war that has rocked the United States’ economy. In many ways, the first thing that Democrats should do when they enter the next Congress is pass a law getting rid of all the Trump tariffs, right? They’re brought into Congress to fix affordability and the tariffs are an affordability problem, and now we’re going to rush into a trade war with China because we might ask the Dutch government to restrict ASML chip making machines. That seems very fraught to say, “We need to enter into an even more heated AI war with China that might result in the Chinese government placing export controls on the goods that you already find unaffordable.” Do you think that there’s the political will to go through this whole exercise, or is it just to punish Nvidia and Jensen Huang? In some ways, this is happening against the backdrop of other issues that are probably more top of mind for both voters and for incoming legislators in the Capitol. Things like cost of living, as you point out, tariffs, and trying to investigate the Trump administration more broadly for corruption and other issues. Somewhere in there is also the debate around data centers and AI itself. So in some ways, I’ll be curious to see how far this goes, the particular Nvidia issue. There is a scenario where a congressional investigation comes and goes, potentially finds no wrongdoing on Jensen Huang’s part, and then this is just folded into the longer debate around export controls. But there’s another world where if there are issues that come up, that could be potentially disruptive, not just for Nvidia and not just for the US-China relationship, but also for the AI boom in the US overall. Tell me more about China itself. You mentioned that their chips will maybe get good enough. There’s an argument that the models right now, the frontier models we have today, are actually good enough to disrupt the economy. They’re certainly good enough to disrupt the field of mathematics. You could stop training new models and just let the technology diffuse and you would still disrupt huge swaths of the economy today. We’re nowhere close to that actually happening. I think the AI labs should prove that they can do it with the technology they have today. That’s for another time. But China doesn’t need to compete at the frontier to gain the productivity advantages and to gain the industrial advantages. The example I keep using is 5G. I was told for a decade that we had to win the race to 5G, otherwise China would do something and no one would ever tell me what the “something” was. What is the “something” with AI that China will defeat us at that has made this such a critical geopolitical chess match? And is there a point where it will just be good enough for them to achieve that “something”? The funny thing is that China doesn’t see this AI race as being so much about the frontier per se. They’re really much more focused on diffusing the technology. And they think they can “win” the AI race by just having AI used much more broadly and integrated throughout the economy, especially in areas like manufacturing where they are already the behemoth. I think when they see the discussion around getting to AGI, certainly from the government standpoint in Beijing, that to them looks like a bubble and a waste of money. Why are you building all that compute for that? What’s interesting to see is the strategy as they’ve been playing it out is one where they’re trying to not fall too far behind the US, but really focus a lot more on trying to get — especially these open source models — out there across the Chinese economy and globally as well. To that extent, on that metric, they seem to be doing well. That, to me, always has seemed like the real fight. Anthropic and OpenAI are furious that the Chinese companies are constantly distilling their models. They’re trying to build some technology to keep them from distilling their models. But if you believe in the promise of AI and what it can do to the economy, your emphasis should be on diffusing good enough models, not AGI. Whereas our emphasis due to the way our market works is a bunch of guys who think they’re going to build digital Jesus. Whatever is going to happen, that’s the thing they want. [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei has to pretend that he cares about Salesforce, but we know what his real priority is. How do the United States and China compete in that dynamic, where you have one very managed economy that has set a much more near-term and potentially achievable goal, and then our market system where the incentives of the leading market players have nothing to do with the economic incentives of the rest of us? There’s even an ideological foundation to all of this because the vision of AGI is one that is so deeply embedded right now in the American AI community and Silicon Valley culture that I think there’s a risk of potential disconnect, not just between the US and China on this issue, but also within the US, between those who are in the labs like Anthropic and those who are outside who are saying, “Why are we building these giant metal boxes in our backyards? We don’t really see the point of this.” So there’s already that divergence there. Part of it is this longstanding obsession in the American AI imagination with getting to the machine god essentially. Bringing that all back to the context of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, Alice Huang, and Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a data center provider in Southeast Asia. It’s theoretically their business. They’re building data centers, they’re buying these chips. Shouldn’t market forces just end this? The United States AI companies want to build data centers. They will pay whatever rates because they have an ideological purpose that is disconnected from capitalism potentially. The Chinese government is just trying to diffuse AI into manufacturing and the United States government would like to hold them back. Shouldn’t market forces just mean that you sell the chips to the highest bidder and the highest bidder will almost always be an American AI company? That’s an interesting question, because there is ultimately market demand in China still for these Nvidia chips. And there’s a divergence here between the companies in China who still want access to Nvidia chips and the government who is saying, “No, no, no. Why don’t you try Chinese chips? Why don’t you help us with our Chinese domestic chip development?” There’s that divergence there. What’s interesting is players like Megaspeed in between could potentially do things like not just allow Chinese AI companies, again, to potentially get access to Nvidia chips, but then the argument some people are making is that those are chips that could have gone to the US AI companies and hyperscalers who are desperate. That is an argument that’s out there, but fundamentally, I don’t know how much of this is driven by those sheer commercial interests alone or, again, by some of these policy or ideological divides. Or by the influence of an alleged spy. Right, exactly. Because in a pure market environment, I think I know how this goes, but then you obviously have the complicated geopolitical dynamics and then you have this corruption element where both governments are attempting to influence one company at the center of the storm. What do you think happens if the Nvidia board investigation determines that Jensen acted inappropriately or a shareholder lawsuit imposes massive liability on Nvidia or a congressional investigation? There’s no way this company comes out of this unscathed, and the options are Jensen steps down or Nvidia’s restrained in some way or export controls go up even higher. Walk us through the probabilities and what you think happens next. There is a scenario actually where this ends up with not that much happening. Interesting. There is a pathway where there is a congressional investigation and they possibly find no wrongdoing or maybe Jensen really didn’t know, as he claims, that this Alice Huang person was a Chinese spy, and that this ends up feeding into the longer standing trajectory of all the export control debates and everything like that. That’s one possibility. Another possibility, though, is if there is some kind of wrongdoing that’s found, Jensen Huang might have to step down as CEO. He’s not just like a central node, he is like American AI, like the pillar that is holy. He’s the only one making the dollar. I mean, this is very important. Yeah, it’s like if you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that. If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that. The question becomes, if he were no longer the CEO of Nvidia, how much impact would that have on Nvidia’s ability to make progress on its own AI chips and what impact would that have on the rest of the US AI industry? One possibility, for example, is that there is a slowdown in Nvidia’s ability to crank out next generation after next generation of better and better chips. And that could impact US overall compute build out. That is one possibility. Another possibility is that there’s just so much demand and that the knowledge is diffused enough throughout Nvidia that the company can still continue to make progress at a breakneck pace even without their fearless leader at the top. A lot is unknown. “Fearless” is the right word, because when I look at Nvidia, again, I don’t think Jensen is designing the chips. I know that there’s a character he wants to play, where he’s in all the meetings and he’s probably taking some risk in chip design that is hard for us to see from the outside. But what we can see is Jensen’s enormous appetite for risk when it comes to financing neoclouds and investing in frontier AI companies. All of the dollars Nvidia is making flow back out in a circle to the AI ecosystem. It’s unclear to me whether that continues to happen without Jensen specifically being willing to front the risk and show up on CNBC as the face of the risk and say, “Everything’s okay.” What do you think happens then? His role as not just a technology leader, but as a market maker is really crucial. When he calls out certain companies like certain startups or neoclouds, you can see their stock prices go up. When he says something like, “I don’t know if this quantum thing is going to work out,” you saw the entire industry takes a hit. So that is the weight of his role in the broader ecosystem. Going forward, without that kind of advocate and this market maker playing this active role, that’s another factor. Beyond the Nvidia chips themselves and the technological role of the company, there is this deeper industry or even sociological function that Jensen plays and that Nvidia plays in this broader AI buildout. One of the interesting dynamics in all of that is Jensen also doesn’t seem to care very much about AGI. He thinks it’s just software. I’ve heard him say, “This is just software. Everybody calm down. These risks are fake. We don’t need a safety regime, all this stuff.” He’s more aligned with what you’re describing as the Chinese viewpoint, where this is just a tool to accelerate our economy. If he goes, maybe that changes too. It’s possible. He has been one of the most powerful counterweights to the “let’s go all in on AGI” perspective that you hear from Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, for example. Without his voice in that process, he’s also been a very strong advocate for open source. Again, emphasizing the diffusion rather than the, say, control and restrictions on cutting-edge AI. I do think if his voice is not there, there would be a pretty big vacuum for folks who would advocate that position or that view. At the same time though, again, beyond the immediate AI industry in the US, I don’t know how much that “race to AGI” argument resonates with the broader US public. Right now a lot of people are just more wondering about the nuts and bolts of it. Is this technology going to cost me my job tomorrow? Is it actually useful? Is it impacting my university studies? Those are things that maybe are more impactful day-to-day for most ordinary Americans. It is abundantly clear that Jensen is not a great spokesperson to the average consumer in the United States. He has not made the sale to them. He’s made the sale to a bunch of financiers. He’s made the sale to Wall Street. He’s made the sale to the tech industry. But the average American, as we can just see from the polling in the election, is very, very skeptical of all of this and very, very skeptical of the costs versus the benefits. Again, I’m just putting that in the context of there’s an alleged Chinese spy whispering in the ear of this man. What truly would the Chinese government hope to gain from that? Because in one way, they’ve actually achieved a victory here. They’ve destabilized the American AI economy. But it doesn’t seem like that was the goal. They’re furiously denying that any of this even happened. There is another very counterintuitive take, which is they kind of shot themselves in the foot on this one. From Beijing’s perspective, they don’t want to see more export controls, they might want to see a loosening. But now because of this potential Chinese spy, they’ve tainted the one man who has been advocating the most for loosening export controls. In some ways now, they’ve taken out someone who had otherwise for sheer commercial reasons been more aligned, and who’s going to take that place? If anything now, it has really charged the Democrats especially, who have been criticizing the Trump administration about not being tougher on these export controls. It has really galvanized the Democrats on this front and made it more of an issue perhaps than it was before. Yeah, especially when you connect it to corruption and the AI industry wasting money, all this stuff, it’s all there for them. Tell me more broadly about Chinese spying in the AI industry. There was a report, I don’t know, a few months ago that OpenAI was warning its employees that spies abound, that if suddenly attractive people appeared, be wary because they were probably spies. I love that. There’s just something about that that’s great. Obviously when it hits Jensen, it’s a different kind of story, especially with the national security implications and corruption implications. Give us a sense of what the spy trade is like on the ground for the average AI researcher. All I can say here is that they are juicy targets. For the US AI labs, anyone who’s involved with cutting-edge frontier AI, chip production, and chip design would be juicy targets for Chinese intelligence gathering because this is something where China’s trying to catch up. They’re trying to figure out how to keep pace with the US on AI and try to build their own alternatives to Nvidia GPUs. You can see there have been other examples of cases where they’ve been poaching engineers from TSMC in Taiwan or from South Korea, and have struggled to deal with efforts to hold back this strategic IP basically. There’s probably a lot more happening under the surface in terms of this cat-and-mouse game, but I do think that they are prime targets. Correct me if I’m wrong, but I think that there have been warnings from the US government to be careful and to step up your game on the cybersecurity front and the intelligence front to protect against these threats. Meanwhile, they’re putting all their information into Slack and getting breached on the daily. Who knows if these warnings are taking off. Onto the last set of questions here — I’m thinking about Apple and Tesla, where we moved our manufacturing to China and we moved our supply chains to China, the Chinese industries. Whether it was above board or not — and there’s a rich debate you could have on that, we’ve had it on the show — they learned a lot from our companies. There was technology transfer. That’s happening in AI too. There are a lot of Chinese AI researchers working in and around these labs. There is technology transfer happening, again, above board or not. Isn’t that just the normal course of business or is there something more nefarious happening here? To some extent there are people flows and knowledge flows. You might not even think of it in terms of national-level AI communities. You might think about this global diffusion of know-how tips and tricks for squeezing a bit more performance out of the same amount of compute. Especially up until recently, you saw a lot of sharing of, say, papers like the transformer paper, that disseminated new architectural breakthroughs throughout the global AI community. And now that’s changing, obviously, as a lot of companies, especially the US companies, are holding this much closer to their chest. But there is this broader question about who gets access to this. Who gains and loses? I guess it’s also not just a one-way flow. Some of these American AI companies benefit a lot from having some of these Chinese developers work with them. In the same way Apple and Tesla, it wasn’t just like they gave away the crown jewels to China, but that China in turn saved these companies, especially at times when they were facing a perilous moment in their histories. There’s this bigger question about what the line is between normal commercial and technology flows versus a concerted state-backed effort to obtain sensitive strategic secrets and IP technology that would have broader geopolitical implications. Does that strategy for China look like a bunch of companies like Megaspeed with allegedly compromised executives, or does it play out more directly? Actually if anything, it would be less about the companies like Megaspeed, who seem to be middlemen for dealing with compute, and perhaps different companies, different agencies perhaps in the Chinese system, that might be more active. At one extreme you have the outright concerted efforts at industrial espionage. They’re state-backed actors who are very systematic at trying to obtain some of the best commercial secrets from around the world, including from American companies. But on the other hand, you do also have this gray zone of, “If a Chinese company acquires a stake in a US or European company, what does that mean? Does that mean they’re trying to obtain the technology or is that a regular commercial deal?” That’s where it starts to get more difficult to parse and you’d have to look at it on a case-by-case basis. One of the dynamics in talking about the Chinese government and the United States, especially when you talk to American industrialists, is that the American government is chaos and democracy is messy and everyone’s running in 50 different directions, and the Chinese system is directed. They make 100-year plans, not one-quarter plans. We’ve heard it. Everyone knows these cliches. How true is that? In this case alone, it doesn’t seem like they achieved the goal of their plan. In many cases, they might have actually set themselves back. Oh, yeah. For those who actually study China, who have done long-term research on this country and who understand it more closely, it looks like a much messier picture than any of these portrayals, especially from those in Silicon Valley who try to juxtapose China against what they find to be this annoyingly messy and unruly democracy. The Chinese system, both within the government and then across industries and government, is full of conflicting interests, rife with corruption. There are lots of times where you have bureaucratic turf wars that spill out into the open. You have missteps, ones that can backfire profoundly. You see that all the time. You see the local governments not following what Beijing wants, or following what Beijing wants but in the wrong direction. Sometimes they’re given a signal and they say, “Oh, okay, we got to run that way.” And then Beijing says, “No, no, no, no, no, other way, other way.” This happens all the time, and to anyone in Silicon Valley who’s trying to make this “neat” argument, all I can say is, go talk to people in China. They can tell you how messy it actually is on the ground. Kyle, this has been great. What do you think will happen next year? What should people be looking out for? The biggest thing is a congressional investigation and who’s behind that, what that surface is. And then potentially along with that, these pending bills around export controls and whether those will now get more momentum to pass in Congress, and whether Trump himself, and the White House in general, will try to play a role in either stopping that or giving that a quiet green light. I suspect we’re going to want to talk to you again as this process plays out. Thank you so much, Kyle, for being on Decoder. Thank you. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. articles.title: Warren says Huang’s resignation ‘does not absolve him,’ Nvidia
articles.summary: Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said Thursday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation amid mounting controversy regarding his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, “does not absolve him” or the company. “Jensen Huang’s decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for…
articles.body:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said Thursday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation amid mounting controversy regarding his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, “does not absolve him” or the company.

“Jensen Huang’s decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws,” Warren said on social platform X .

“They still owe Congress answers,” she added.

Nvidia announced earlier Thursday that the CEO was resigning immediately and Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia, will take over as interim CEO.

The announcement came after the tech leader was brought into controversy following a New York Times report that claimed American authorities discovered Chinese businessperson Alice Huang illegally smuggled advanced AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with Jensen Huang. On Wednesday, the Times reported Jensen Huang had a separate affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, citing five people who worked at the company.

Following the initial Times report, Nvidia’s board announced Sunday it would initiate an independent investigation into the matter. On Tuesday, the company announced it hired former acting U.S. attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to conduct the investigation.

Prior to that, the tech CEO admitted that he has been unfaithful to his wife, adding, “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” according to a Sunday report from Bloomberg .

He was called to appear by GOP lawmakers in a joint, closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 to address concerns regarding Nvidia’s security protocols and his interactions with the alleged spy.

articles.title: Sentinel at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier awarded medal by Hegseth
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a prestigious medal to an Army sentinel on Thursday who loudly admonished the Pentagon chief and his group at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery for breaking decorum the day before. Hegseth hosted the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, at the Pentagon on Thursday…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a prestigious medal to an Army sentinel on Thursday who loudly admonished the Pentagon chief and his group at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery for breaking decorum the day before .

Hegseth hosted the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, at the Pentagon on Thursday where he “proudly” awarded Spc. Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the “execution of his duties” at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a Pentagon official told The Hill.

The Defense secretary shared the photo Thursday of awarding the medal, which was established in 1963, writing on social platform X, “We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots.”

Hegseth and his senior staff were reprimanded by Iglesias on Wednesday for laughing after they stopped to take photos in front of the tomb at Arlington National Cemetery.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the sentinel yelled.

Decorum is fiercely observed at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, one of the most sacred war memorials in the nation. It marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.

Hegseth was accompanied by his wife, Jennifer Hegseth, his chief of staff, Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.

It is unclear who laughed, but the incident was caught on television and went viral online.

“The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe,” Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement Wednesday.

“While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum,” Parnell said.

Hegseth and his team were part of the wreath-laying ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

articles.title: Building approvals hit digi roadblocks as TN rules await portal update
articles.summary: Chennai builders face approval delays as TN rule changes aren’t updated on the planning portal and CMDA portal glitches stall submissions and clearances.
articles.body: Chennai: Builders in Chennai are facing a double whammy in securing building approvals. On the one hand, local bodies, including Greater Chennai Corporation, have not updated the single-window planning portal’s software to reflect the Tamil Nadu govt’s latest regulatory relaxations; on the other, recurring technical glitches in the Chennai Metropolitan Development Authority’s (CMDA) existing portal are stalling applications at various stages.Developers say the twin problems are defeating the objective of faster clearances, with delays affecting project schedules, increasing financing costs and holding up new launches.Nearly a month ago, the govt rolled out GOs 179, 180, and 194, introduced third-party certification, enhanced the approval powers of local bodies, and increased permissible building heights in certain categories. However, the changes are yet to be incorporated into the online planning permission system.GO 179 allows registered architects and Grade-I engineers to certify specified residential, commercial and industrial buildings. GO 180 delegates approval powers to local bodies for residential projects up to 1,500sqm FSI and commercial buildings up to 500sqm FSI. GO 194 revises building height limits from 18.3m to 19.5m and amends road width, setback and parking rules.“The govt should have updated the software of the portal before rolling out the portal. More than 1,000 proposals are stuck in limbo. We are unable to submit proposals under the revised provisions and access the intended relaxations,” S Ramaprabhu, from the Builders’ Association of India (BAI).Greater Chennai Corporation commissioner G S Sameeran said that the update will be done soon.Meanwhile, developers are facing problems with CMDA’s existing online approval system. CREDAI Chennai, in a representation dated Oct 26 to CMDA, listed technical difficulties involving application submission, uploading documents and revised drawings, statutory NOCs, payment of charges, and tracking application status. It also flagged delays in completion certificate acknowledgements and access to essential services.“The glitches are recurring and are not confined to particular applications. Problems persist at almost every stage-initial submission, scrutiny, fee payment, receipt generation, digital signature and issue of planning permission, as well as completion certificate applications and their subsequent approval,” said a developer.He added that even after obtaining completion certificates, developers approaching the Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (CMWSSB) for connections are being told that infrastructure development charges payable by CMDA have not been transferred. “The govt has to intervene ensure that applicants are not charged interest or penalties when delays are caused solely by technical failures of the portal or related systems,” he added.A senior CMDA official said that a special team headed by the chief planner and senior planner - e -governance - has been formed to sort out the issues. “In parallel, we are also floating a tender for a new AI-based online PPA,” the official added.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: American Cancer Society recommends regular prostate cancer testing in updated guidelines
articles.summary: The American Cancer Society released an updated guideline Thursday that recommends regular prostate cancer screening for average-risk men between the ages of 50-69 years old. The society also recommended annual screening starting at the age of 45 for “Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer,” according to a press release…
articles.body:
The American Cancer Society released an updated guideline Thursday that recommends regular prostate cancer screening for average-risk men between the ages of 50-69 years old.

The society also recommended annual screening starting at the age of 45 for “Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer,” according to a press release announcing the updated guidelines .

They also added that for men aged 70-74, “individualized decision-making on continuing screening is recommended.”

“Think of prostate cancer screening as an early warning system for your health,” said Shanthi Sivendran, interim chief patient officer for the American Cancer Society in the release. “By catching aggressive cancers with a simple PSA blood test, you open the door to highly effective treatments that protect your future. Meanwhile, lower-risk findings can be safely managed through careful, active surveillance.”

The discussion surrounding prostate cancer has been brought into the political spotlight following former President Biden’s diagnosis in May last year . Biden was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer with bone metastasis, though doctors said his cancer was “hormone sensitive which allows for effective management.” He completed his treatment in October 2025.

“I know firsthand the toll of this disease, and I know that catching it early saves lives,” Biden wrote in a post on X following the announcement of the updated guidelines. “So talk to your doctor, get screened, and let’s keep working to end cancer as we know it.”

On Sunday, the former president said in a statement that he would be scaling back on events promoting his upcoming presidential memoir , “Promise Me, America,” scheduled to be released on Nov. 17. He talked about his diagnosis while working on the book.

“Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me,” Biden wrote in his statement. “But sometimes it slows me down. What that means is, unfortunately, I won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped. However, I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves.”

In a People Magazine interview published Wednesday , the former president said he did not hide his cancer diagnosis while he was in the White House. When asked about some public accusations of him hiding the diagnosis while in office, Biden said, “A lot of people do that” but he “didn’t do that. We let the public know when I found out, when I knew what was going on.”
